Setup

One operator,
the whole line

Most projects get handed down a line — strategy to design, design to 3D, 3D to production, production to web. I've stood at every one of those stations. That means a brief can go from a sentence to a finished asset without a handoff quietly losing the point of it.

For a decade I ran the marketing and communications department at an industry-leading manufacturer. That taught me the strategic half: positioning, market research, product launches, budgets, and building a team people actually wanted to be on. The making never stopped alongside it — I was still the one drawing the mark, lighting the render, and writing the CSS.

That range keeps widening, and right now it's pointed at AI — running and customizing models locally and in the cloud, and building software with them. Vector art turns into CNC toolpaths. Product ideas turn into shipped software. Same instinct every time: learn the machine, then use it properly.

T01Thumbnails & social creative

The click
is the job

A thumbnail competes against twenty others in a grid the size of a business card. One subject, one idea, faces and type big enough to survive the crop — and enough curiosity left over to earn the click.

YouTube thumbnails
T02Product design & interface

Products,
not mockups

A run of spreadsheet-based tools designed, built and sold end to end — expense trackers for bachelor and bachelorette parties, a subscription tracker, a classroom timer, group travel tools. I did the product thinking, the interface, the theming, the listing art and the support docs.

T03Brand marks & logotypes

Marks

A logo has to survive being shrunk to a favicon, embroidered on a hat, and cut out of plywood. These were all drawn as vectors for exactly that reason — one shape that still reads at any size, in one colour, at a glance.

T04Identity systems & composites

Identity
in use

A mark on its own is a shape. It becomes a brand once there's a palette, a type system, a banner, a product shot and a tone of voice sitting behind it — and once every one of those pieces agrees with the others.

T05Vector & technical illustration

Drawn to
spec

Product diagrams, cutaways and signage — built with points and curves so they can be scaled to a trade-show wall, recoloured for a new model year, or handed straight to a cutter without redrawing a thing.

T063D modelling, lighting & rendering

Built in
the box

Photography needs a finished product, a studio and a day. A render needs a model and a light rig — and it can show a configuration that doesn't physically exist yet. Modelled, shaded, lit and composited for launch material and catalogue work.

T07CNC · CAM · toolpath generation

Telling the
machine how

Drawing the part is half of it. The other half is explaining it to a machine: choose the cutter, set feeds and speeds, decide stepover and depth of cut, order the operations, and generate a toolpath that leaves a clean edge instead of a burnt one.

CAM · Pocket + contour · Tool 3 

      

      

        
Vector artwork is already halfway to a toolpath. The same curves I
          draw for a logo can drive a profile cut; the same surfaces I model for a render can drive a finishing
          pass. Signage, inlays, panels, jigs, one-off parts — CAD to CAM to chips on the floor, with the setup
          sheet written as carefully as the artwork.

T09Software, web & interactive prototypes

      
Demo
software

      
CaribooDash — a concept for a convenience store that drives to you: a stocked vehicle
        roaming Williams Lake, with customers seeing live inventory and live location. I designed and built both
        halves as working prototypes, the customer app and the driver's operations console. Both are interactive
        right here, or open them full screen.

    

    

      

        

          
Customer app

          
Browse what's physically on the truck right now, watch it move on the map, build an order and track it

T10Artificial intelligence — deploy, customize, build

      
Where I'm
pointed now

      
The newest machine in the shop, and the one I've gone deepest on: what these models
        can actually do, how to run them on your own hardware and in the cloud, how to customize them for a
        specific job, and how to program with them instead of around them.

    

    

      

        

          Inference · routing · deployment
          
        

      

      

        
In practice that means picking the right model for the task instead
          of the biggest one, getting it running privately when the data shouldn't leave the building, giving it
          the context and tools it needs to be useful, and wiring the whole thing into work that actually ships.
          It has changed how fast an idea gets from a sentence to a working thing.
